bib.title: Asking and Answering Questions to Evaluate the Factual Consistency of Summaries
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pages 5008-5020

question: Can asking questions about a summary and answering them from both summary and source give an automatic metric that tracks human judgments of factual consistency better than n-gram metrics?
hypothesis: If a summary is factually consistent with its source, questions asked about the summary receive similar answers from the summary and the source.
contributions: QAGS, an automatic model-based metric for factual consistency of generated text
New human judgments of factual consistency of model summaries for CNN/DM and XSUM
Ablations showing robustness to model quality, domain mismatch and number of questions
Analysis of generated questions and answers showing which summary parts are inconsistent

method.summary: QAGS generates K=20 questions from a summary with an answer-conditional BART QG model fine-tuned on NewsQA, answers each with a BERT-large extractive QA model fine-tuned on SQuAD2.0 from both source and summary, and averages token-level F1 between the two answers. It is validated by Pearson correlation with MTurk sentence-level consistency judgments.
method.task: factual consistency evaluation of abstractive summarization

datasets.name: CNN/DM summaries (Gehrmann et al. 2018 outputs)
datasets.source: Hermann et al. 2015; Nallapati et al. 2016

datasets.name: XSUM BART outputs
datasets.source: Narayan et al. 2018; BART fine-tuned on XSUM (Lewis et al. 2019)
datasets.preprocessing: summary prepended back to the article for humans and QAGS, because summaries contain facts (e.g. first names) absent from the article

datasets.name: NewsQA
datasets.source: Trischler et al. 2017; CNN articles with crowdsourced questions
datasets.preprocessing: answer concatenated to article with marker token, then marker token and question

datasets.name: SQuAD2.0
datasets.split: dev set used for model selection and F1

datasets.name: Falke et al. (2019) sentence ranking
datasets.source: Falke et al. 2019; summary sentences from Chen and Bansal (2018) model

training.objective: QG: label-smoothed cross entropy, smoothing 0.1; QA: extractive span with unanswerable (SQuAD2.0)

other.checkpoint: QG best dev perplexity; QA best dev performance
other.note: QG uses the same hyperparameters as the original BART work

inference.decoding: QG: beam search width 10, length penalty 1.0, trigram repetition blocking, min length 8, max length 60
inference.samples: 10 answer candidates x 10 beams = 100 question candidates per summary; K=20 kept; no repeated runs or seeds stated

parameters.answer_candidates: 10 named entities and noun phrases per summary from spaCy en-web-sm; randomly sample 10 if more, duplicate if fewer
parameters.question_filters: drop text after first question mark, exact duplicates, questions under 3 tokens, questions the QA model deems unanswerable or answers differently than expected; top 20 by probability, random sample of filtered if too few

other.sampling: top-k and top-p tried, questions diverse but noisy and nongrammatical

metrics.name: Pearson correlation with human consistency
metrics.definition: summary-level; human score = mean over summary sentences of majority vote of 3 binary annotations

metrics.name: Sentence ranking accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of triplets where the consistent sentence is ranked above the inconsistent one

eval.protocol: MTurk (via ParlAI), US workers with >=1000 approved HITs and >=98% acceptance; 3 annotations per summary, sentence-by-sentence binary; checks: time under 30s fails, attention checks, explanation per sentence; $0.15 base + $0.85 bonus ($1.00 per summary). Significance of correlations p<.01 (CNN/DM), p<.05 (XSUM).

evidence.quote: After ﬁltering, we use the K = 20 most probable questions.

limits: Measures only factual inconsistency against the source, not fluency, readability or factual recall; authors recommend using it with complementary metrics
QG and QA choices are specific to abstractive summarization and may need adaptation elsewhere
Authors expect extractive summarizers to obtain nearly perfect QAGS scores (stated as expectation, not measured)
Answer candidates are named entities and noun phrases, so mostly entity errors are caught
Extractive QA cannot match paraphrases; F1 fails on lexical variation
Only 235 and 239 summaries, one model per dataset; inter-annotator alpha 0.51 and 0.34
Ablation uses BERT QA, a strong baseline; weaker QA might drop more
No seeds, repeated runs or confidence intervals reported; QG batch size, hardware, compute not given
XSUM correlations are low for all metrics (QAGS 17.49) and XSUM ablations show no clear trend

terms.definition: Question Answering and Generation for Summarization, a metric for factual consistency of abstractive summaries

figures.caption: Overview of QAGS. A set of questions is generated based on the summary. The questions are then answered using both the source article and the summary. Corresponding answers are compared using a similarity function and averaged across questions to produce the final QAGS score.
